Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Anaís Hernández had always been driven to help others. As a community organizer in her predominantly Latin American neighborhood, she spent most of her days advocating for social justice and empowering marginalized voices. But despite her tough exterior, Anaís harbored a secret: she was still trapped by the memories of her childhood. When Anaís was just 10 years old, her mother's boyfriend had beaten her mercilessly in their small apartment. The sounds of shattering glass and her own screams were etched into her mind like a grotesque painting. Some moments were crystal clear – the feeling of her body flying across the room, the taste of blood on her lips – while others remained frustratingly blank. Even now, Anaís couldn't recall what had led up to that fateful night or how it had ended. As she grew older, Anaís began to develop strategies to cope with these fragmented memories. She would often sit with her back against a wall, surveying the room as if waiting for an attack. At work, she'd position herself near the door, just in case she needed to make a quick escape. Her friends and colleagues might have seen it as a quirk, but Anaís knew that this was the only way she could feel safe. But safety was a fleeting concept for Anaís. Even when surrounded by loved ones or immersed in her work, she'd suddenly be jolted back to that night. A memory would surface – the sensation of being trapped, the feeling of having no options – and Anaís would freeze. Her mind would go numb, as if observing herself from afar. In those moments, she felt like a weak person, unable to defend herself or anyone else. Anaís tried to push these memories away by overworking herself. She'd take on more projects, pour her energy into meetings and rallies, anything to keep her mind occupied. But at night, when the world outside grew quiet, Anaís's vigilance kicked in. She'd lie awake for hours, listening for any sign of intruders, checking behind her every few minutes as if someone was lurking just out of sight. As a result, Anaís began to pull away from those closest to her. Her partner would try to initiate intimate conversations, but Anaís would shut down, feeling dead inside. She'd tell herself that others – stronger, braver people – would have stopped the abuse or escaped their circumstances with ease. Why couldn't she? The shame and self-doubt had been building for years, until one day, Anaís realized that her coping mechanisms were no longer working. The memories still lingered, but now they were accompanied by a creeping sense of dread. What if someone else she loved got hurt? What if she failed to protect them? These questions swirled in Anaís's mind like a vortex, pulling her under. It was this fear – the fear of being powerless and vulnerable – that finally led Anaís to seek help. She knew it wouldn't be easy, but she couldn't shake the feeling that there must be more to life than constantly looking over her shoulder, waiting for the other shoe to drop. As she sat in the therapist's office, back against the wall, Anaís began to whisper a tentative hope: maybe, just maybe, she could learn to confront these memories and find a way out of the darkness that had haunted her for so long.
